arXiv:1802.04685v2 [math.AC] 20 Feb 2018

The two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture

Vered Moskowicz Address: Department of Mathematics, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat-Gan 52900, Israel. Email address: vered.moskowicz@gmail.com
Abstract.

A result by C. C.-A. Cheng, J. H. Mckay and S. S.-S. Wang says the following: Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈ℂ∗\Jac(A,B)\in\mathbb{C}^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈ℂ⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]. Then w∈ℂ⁡[A]w\in\mathbb{C}[A].

We show that in CMW’s result it is possible to replace ℂ\mathbb{C} by any field of characteristic zero, and we conjecture the following ’two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over DD’: Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈D∗\Jac(A,B)\in D^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈D⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in D[x,y], DD is an integral domain of characteristic zero. Then w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A].

We show that if the famous two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture is true, then the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture is true.

Key words and phrases: 
Jacobian Conjecture, Jacobian mate, automorphism pair, Dixmier Conjecture, Weyl algebras, Centralizers
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14R15, 16W20; Secondary 13F20, 16S32

1  Introduction

Throughout this note, kk denotes a field of characteristic zero, DD denotes an integral domain of characteristic zero (DD is commutative) with field of fractions Q⁡(D)Q(D). The group of invertible elements of a ring RR will be denoted by R∗R^{*}.

In  [6, Theorem 1], C. C.-A. Cheng, J. H. Mckay and S. S.-S. Wang have shown that ‘the centralizer with respect to the Jacobian’ of an element A∈ℂ⁡[x,y]A\in\mathbb{C}[x,y] which has a Jacobian mate, equals the polynomial ring in AA over ℂ\mathbb{C}: Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈ℂ∗\Jac(A,B)\in\mathbb{C}^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈ℂ⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]. Then w∈ℂ⁡[A]w\in\mathbb{C}[A].

We show that ℂ\mathbb{C} can be replaced by kk.

Then we conjecture that kk can be replaced by any integral domain of characteristic zero, and call this ’the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over DD’: Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈D∗\Jac(A,B)\in D^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈D⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in D[x,y]. Then w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A].

The famous two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture says that every kk-algebra endomorphism f:(x,y)↦(p,q)f:(x,y)\mapsto(p,q) of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] having an invertible Jacobian, Jac⁡(p,q):=px​qy−py​qx∈k​[x,y]∗=k∗\Jac(p,q):=p_{x}q_{y}-p_{y}q_{x}\in k[x,y]^{*}=k^{*}, is an automorphism of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y]; it was raised by O. H. Keller  [13], actually over ℤ\mathbb{Z} not over kk.

We show that if the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture is true then the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture is true. Therefore, if the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture is false for some DD, then the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture is false. We ’believe’ that the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture is true, so there should be no counterexample to the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture.

2  CMW’s theorem over kk

We will show in two ways that in CMW’s theorem it is possible to replace ℂ\mathbb{C} by kk.

2.1  First way: Independent of the original CMW’s theorem

We will apply the following observation of E. Formanek.

Proposition 2.1 (Formanek’s observation).

Let FF be any field. Assume that C,D∈F⁡[x,y]C,D\in F[x,y] are algebraically dependent over FF. Then there exist h∈F⁡[x,y]h\in F[x,y] and u⁡(t),v⁡(t)∈F⁡[t]u(t),v(t)\in F[t], such that C=u⁡(h)C=u(h) and D=v⁡(h)D=v(h).

Proof.

The proof of Formanek can be found in  [16]. We wish to mention that it uses Lüroth’s theorem, a sharpening of E. Noether (characteristic zero) and A. Schinzel (arbitrary field); those three results can be found in  [20, first chapter]. ∎

The following is a known result due to Jacobi (1841); we will only need the second statement of it.

Theorem 2.2 (Jacobi’s theorem).

Let FF be any field, C,D∈F⁡[x,y]C,D\in F[x,y].

  • (1)

    If CC and DD are algebraically dependent over FF, then Jac⁡(C,D)=0\Jac(C,D)=0.

  • (2)

    Assume that FF is of characteristic zero. If Jac⁡(C,D)=0\Jac(C,D)=0, then CC and DD are algebraically dependent over FF.

Proof.

See  [19, page 8] or  [14, pages 19-20]. ∎

Actually, in (2)(2) of Jacobi’s theorem, the base field FF can be either a field of characteristic zero or a field of large enough characteristic, as is shortly explained in  [19, page 8]. However, we are only interested in the zero characteristic case, since we are interested in the (two-dimensional) Jacobian Conjecture, which has a counterexample over a field of prime characteristic PP, for example, (x,y)↦(x+xP,y)(x,y)\mapsto(x+x^{P},y).

Now we are ready to prove CMW’s result over kk:

Theorem 2.3 (CMW’s theorem over kk).

Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈k∗\Jac(A,B)\in k^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈k⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in k[x,y]. Then w∈k⁡[A]w\in k[A].

Proof.

Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0, so by Jacobi’s theorem, Theorem 2.2 (2)(2), we obtain that AA and ww are algebraically dependent over kk.

By Formanek’s observation, Proposition 2.1, applied to AA and ww we obtain that there exist h∈k⁡[x,y]h\in k[x,y] and u⁡(t),v⁡(t)∈k⁡[t]u(t),v(t)\in k[t], such that A=u⁡(h)A=u(h) and w=v⁡(h)w=v(h).

Then, u′​(h)​Jac⁡(h,B)=Jac⁡(u⁡(h),B)=Jac⁡(A,B)∈k∗u^{\prime}(h)\Jac(h,B)=\Jac(u(h),B)=\Jac(A,B)\in k^{*}, where the first equality can be easily proved. Therefore, u′​(h)∈k∗u^{\prime}(h)\in k^{*} (and Jac⁡(h,B)∈k∗\Jac(h,B)\in k^{*}).

Write u⁡(t)=cm​tm+cm−1​tm−1+⋯+c2​t2+c1​t+c0u(t)=c_{m}t^{m}+c_{m-1}t^{m-1}+\cdots+c_{2}t^{2}+c_{1}t+c_{0}, cj∈kc_{j}\in k, so u′​(t)=m​cm​tm−1+(m−1)​cm−1​tm−2+⋯+2​c2​t+c1u^{\prime}(t)=mc_{m}t^{m-1}+(m-1)c_{m-1}t^{m-2}+\cdots+2c_{2}t+c_{1}, and then u′​(h)=m​cm​hm−1+(m−1)​cm−1​hm−2+⋯+2​c2​h+c1u^{\prime}(h)=mc_{m}h^{m-1}+(m-1)c_{m-1}h^{m-2}+\cdots+2c_{2}h+c_{1}.

From u′​(h)∈k∗u^{\prime}(h)\in k^{*}, we obtain that m​cm​hm−1+(m−1)​cm−1​hm−2+⋯+2​c2​h+c1∈k∗mc_{m}h^{m-1}+(m-1)c_{m-1}h^{m-2}+\cdots+2c_{2}h+c_{1}\in k^{*}, which implies that m​cm=(m−1)​cm−1=…=2​c2=0mc_{m}=(m-1)c_{m-1}=\ldots=2c_{2}=0, c1∈k∗c_{1}\in k^{*}, and c0∈kc_{0}\in k. Since kk is of characteristic zero, we necessarily have cm=cm−1=…=c2=0c_{m}=c_{m-1}=\ldots=c_{2}=0.

Therefore, u⁡(t)=c1​t+c0u(t)=c_{1}t+c_{0}, c1∈k∗c_{1}\in k^{*}, and c0∈kc_{0}\in k, so A=u⁡(h)=c1​h+c0A=u(h)=c_{1}h+c_{0}.

Then, h=A−c0c1h=\frac{A-c_{0}}{c_{1}}, which shows that w=v⁡(h)=v⁡(A−c0c1)∈k⁡[A]w=v(h)=v(\frac{A-c_{0}}{c_{1}})\in k[A]. ∎

The above proof of Theorem 2.3 (which is based on Formanek’s observation) is independent of  [6, Theorem 1], so it can serve as another proof for  [6, Theorem 1].

Our proof of Theorem 2.3 is not valid if we replace kk by a field of large enough characteristic (= a characteristic for which Jacobi’s theorem, Theorem 2.2 (2)(2), is valid); indeed, although Formanek’s observation is valid for any field, we needed zero characteristic for ’j​cj=0jc_{j}=0 implies cj=0c_{j}=0, 2≤j≤m2\leq j\leq m’, and we do not have control on mm.

2.2  Second way: Dependent on the original CMW’s theorem

We can prove CMW’s theorem over kk, Theorem 2.3, in a way which is not based on Formanek’s observation, but it relies on the original proof  [6, Theorem 1]. For convenience, we will divide our proof to three steps:

  • •

    Step 1: Replace ℂ\mathbb{C} by an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

  • •

    Step 2: Prove the result for any sub-field of an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

  • •

    Step 3: Consider kk as a sub-field of k¯\bar{k}, where k¯\bar{k} is an algebraic closure of kk.

Proposition 2.4 (Step 1).

Let LL be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈L∗\Jac(A,B)\in L^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈L⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in L[x,y]. Then w∈L⁡[A]w\in L[A].

Proof.

The proof of the original CMW’s theorem  [6, Theorem 1] is still valid if we replace ℂ\mathbb{C} by LL. Indeed, that proof uses three results: Jacobi’s theorem, Theorem 2.2 (1)(1),  [22, Theorem 1] and  [2, Corollary 1.5, p. 74]. In order to replace ℂ\mathbb{C} by any algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, it is enough to check that each of these three results are valid over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero; indeed:

  • •

    Theorem 2.2 (1)(1) is over any field.

  • •

    [22, Theorem 1] is over any ring.

  • •

    [2, Corollary 1.5, p. 74] is over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

∎

Proposition 2.5 (Step 2).

Let LL be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let K⊆LK\subseteq L be any sub-field of LL.

Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈K∗\Jac(A,B)\in K^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈K⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in K[x,y]. Then w∈K⁡[A]w\in K[A].

Now we present a second proof for CMW’s theorem over kk, Theorem 2.3:

Proposition 2.6 (Step 3, second proof for CMW’s theorem over kk).

Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈k∗\Jac(A,B)\in k^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈k⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in k[x,y]. Then w∈k⁡[A]w\in k[A].

Proof.

Let k¯\bar{k} be an algebraic closure of kk. We have, k⊆k¯k\subseteq\bar{k} with k¯\bar{k} an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Apply Proposition 2.5 and get that w∈k⁡[A]w\in k[A]. ∎

3  The two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture

For u,v∈R⁡[x,y]u,v\in R[x,y], RR a commutative ring, we will use the following usual terminology:

  • •

    If Jac⁡(u,v)∈R​[x,y]∗=R∗\Jac(u,v)\in R[x,y]^{*}=R^{*}, then we say that uu has a Jacobian mate in R⁡[x,y]R[x,y], vv (and vice versa), and u,vu,v is a Jacobian pair (in R⁡[x,y]R[x,y]).

  • •

    If (x,y)↦(u,v)(x,y)\mapsto(u,v) is an automorphism of R⁡[x,y]R[x,y], then we say that u,vu,v is an automorphism pair (in R⁡[x,y]R[x,y]). (An automorphism pair is a Jacobian pair, since the Jacobian of an automorphism pair is invertible in R⁡[x,y]R[x,y]).

Also, we will use the following non-usual terminology: If Jac⁡(u,v)=0\Jac(u,v)=0, then we say that vv is in ’the centralizer of uu with respect to the Jacobian’, uu is in ’the centralizer of vv with respect to the Jacobian’, and u,vu,v ’commute with respect to the Jacobian’.

From CMW’s theorem over kk, Theorem 2.3 or Proposition 2.6, it is immediate to obtain the following:

Theorem 3.1.

Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈D​[x,y]∗=D∗\Jac(A,B)\in D[x,y]^{*}=D^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for

A,B,w∈D⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in D[x,y]. Then w∈Q​(D)​[A]w\in Q(D)[A].

Proof.

A,B∈D⁡[x,y]⊂Q⁡(D)​[x,y]A,B\in D[x,y]\subset Q(D)[x,y] satisfy Jac⁡(A,B)∈D∗⊂Q​(D)∗\Jac(A,B)\in D^{*}\subset Q(D)^{*} and w∈D⁡[x,y]⊂Q⁡(D)​[x,y]w\in D[x,y]\subset Q(D)[x,y] satisfies Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0. We can apply Theorem 2.3 or Proposition 2.6 (Q⁡(D)Q(D) is a field of characteristic zero) and obtain that w∈Q​(D)​[A]w\in Q(D)[A]. ∎

Theorem 3.1 shows that there exists d⁡(w)∈Dd(w)\in D such that d⁡(w)​w∈D⁡[A]d(w)w\in D[A]; indeed, since w∈Q​(D)​[A]w\in Q(D)[A] we can write w=∑λiμi​Aiw=\sum\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}A^{i}, for some 0≠μi,λi∈D0\neq\mu_{i},\lambda_{i}\in D. Then, w=1d​∑di​Aiw=\frac{1}{d}\sum d_{i}A^{i}, where d=∏μi∈D∗d=\prod{\mu_{i}}\in D^{*} and dj=λj​∏μiμj∈Dd_{j}=\frac{\lambda_{j}\prod{\mu_{i}}}{\mu_{j}}\in D. Therefore, d​w=d⁡(1d​∑di​Ai)=d​1d​(∑di​Ai)=∑di​Ai∈D⁡[A]dw=d(\frac{1}{d}\sum d_{i}A^{i})=d\frac{1}{d}(\sum d_{i}A^{i})=\sum d_{i}A^{i}\in D[A]. This does not tell much, since each ww has its own d=d⁡(w)d=d(w), so in order to obtain the centralizer of AA with respect to the Jacobian, we will need to add (apriori) infinitely many 1d⁡(w)\frac{1}{d(w)}’s to DD. In other words, we can say that the centralizer of AA is D⁡[{1d⁡(w)}w]​[A]⊆Q⁡(D)​[A]D[\{\frac{1}{d(w)}\}_{w}][A]\subseteq Q(D)[A]. We conjecture that the centralizer of AA is the smallest possible (= every 1d⁡(w)\frac{1}{d(w)} belongs to DD), namely D⁡[A]D[A].

Conjecture 3.2 (The two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over DD).

Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈D​[x,y]∗=D∗\Jac(A,B)\in D[x,y]^{*}=D^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈D⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in D[x,y]. Then w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A].

Examples 3.3 (Non-counterexamples).

First non-counterexample: The following is not a counterexample to the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over ℤ\mathbb{Z}: A=2+3​yA=2+3y, w=1+yw=1+y; clearly ww is in the centralizer of AA w.r.t. the Jacobian, and w=1+y=13+13​(2+3​y)=13+13​A∈ℚ⁡[A]−ℤ⁡[A]w=1+y=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}(2+3y)=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}A\in\mathbb{Q}[A]-\mathbb{Z}[A]. However, AA does not have a Jacobian mate in ℤ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{Z}[x,y], since if B∈ℤ⁡[x,y]B\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y] was a Jacobian mate of AA, then, by definition, −3​Bx=Jac⁡(A,B)∈ℤ​[x,y]∗=ℤ∗={1,−1}-3B_{x}=\Jac(A,B)\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]^{*}=\mathbb{Z}^{*}=\{1,-1\} (BxB_{x} denotes the derivative of BB w.r.t. xx), so Bx=±13∉ℤ⁡[x,y]B_{x}=\pm\frac{1}{3}\notin\mathbb{Z}[x,y], which is impossible (since B∈ℤ⁡[x,y]B\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y] implies that Bx∈ℤ⁡[x,y]B_{x}\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]).

Second non-counterexample: The following is not a counterexample to the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over D:=k⁡[a2,a​b,b2,a3,b3]D:=k[a^{2},ab,b^{2},a^{3},b^{3}], where aa and bb are transcendental over kk; it is due to YCor  [17]: A=(a​x+b​y)2=a2​x2+2​a​b​x​y+b2​y2∈D⁡[x,y]A=(ax+by)^{2}=a^{2}x^{2}+2abxy+b^{2}y^{2}\in D[x,y], w=(a​x+b​y)3=a3​x3+3​a2​b​x2​y+3​a​b2​x​y2+b3​y3w=(ax+by)^{3}=a^{3}x^{3}+3a^{2}bx^{2}y+3ab^{2}xy^{2}+b^{3}y^{3}; clearly ww is in the centralizer of AA w.r.t. the Jacobian. From considerations of degrees, w∉D⁡[A]w\notin D[A] and also from considerations of degrees, w∉Q​(D)​[A]w\notin Q(D)[A] (the degree of ww is 33, while the degree of a polynomial in AA is even). However, AA does not have a Jacobian mate in D⁡[x,y]D[x,y]; this can be seen in two ways:

  • •

    Otherwise, by Theorem 3.1, w∈Q​(D)​[A]w\in Q(D)[A], but w∉Q​(D)​[A]w\notin Q(D)[A].

  • •

    Otherwise, if B∈D⁡[x,y]B\in D[x,y] was a Jacobian mate of AA, then, by definition, Jac⁡(A,B)∈D​[x,y]∗=D∗=k∗\Jac(A,B)\in D[x,y]^{*}=D^{*}=k^{*} A direct computation shows that 12​Jac⁡(A,B)=(a2​x+a​b​y)​By−(b2​y+a​b​x)​Bx\frac{1}{2}\Jac(A,B)=(a^{2}x+aby)B_{y}-(b^{2}y+abx)B_{x}, hence Jac⁡(A,B)|(x=0,y=0)=0\Jac(A,B)|(x=0,y=0)=0, which contradicts Jac⁡(A,B)∈k∗\Jac(A,B)\in k^{*}.

The two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture has a positive answer (at least) in the following two special cases:

  • •

    First special case: DD is, in addition, a field; this is CMW’s theorem over kk, Theorem 2.3 or Proposition 2.6.

  • •

    Second special case: (x,y)↦(A,B)(x,y)\mapsto(A,B) is, in addition, an automorphism (A,BA,B is an automorphism pair); this is the content of the following Theorem 3.4.

Theorem 3.4 (Special case: Automorphism pair).

Suppose Jac⁡(A,B)∈D​[x,y]∗=D∗\Jac(A,B)\in D[x,y]^{*}=D^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈D⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in D[x,y]. Further assume that (x,y)↦(A,B)(x,y)\mapsto(A,B) is an automorphism of D⁡[x,y]D[x,y]. Then w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A].

Proof.

Denote g:(x,y)↦(A,B)g:(x,y)\mapsto(A,B). By assumption, gg is an automorphism of D⁡[x,y]D[x,y], so g−1:D⁡[x,y]→D⁡[x,y]g^{-1}:D[x,y]\to D[x,y] exists and is also an automorphism of D⁡[x,y]D[x,y].

First step A=xA=x: If A=xA=x, then it is easy to see that w∈D⁡[A]=D⁡[x]w\in D[A]=D[x]. Indeed, wy=Jac⁡(x,w)=Jac⁡(A,w)=0w_{y}=\Jac(x,w)=\Jac(A,w)=0, where wyw_{y} is the derivative of ww with respect to yy. Write ww in its (0,1)(0,1)-degree form: w=w0+w1​y+w2​y2+⋯+wm​ymw=w_{0}+w_{1}y+w_{2}y^{2}+\cdots+w_{m}y^{m}, where w0,w1,w2,…,wm∈D⁡[x]w_{0},w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{m}\in D[x]. We have just seen that wy=0w_{y}=0, hence, 0=wy=w1+2​w2​y+⋯+m​wm​ym−10=w_{y}=w_{1}+2w_{2}y+\cdots+mw_{m}y^{m-1}, which implies that w1=2​w2=…=m​wm=0w_{1}=2w_{2}=\ldots=mw_{m}=0, so w1=w2=…=wm=0w_{1}=w_{2}=\ldots=w_{m}=0 (since the characteristic of DD is zero). Therefore, w=w0∈D⁡[x]=D⁡[A]w=w_{0}\in D[x]=D[A], and we are done.

Second step AA arbitrary: The general case can be obtained from the special case A=xA=x.

Claim: u:=g−1​(w)u:=g^{-1}(w) is in the centralizer of xx. Proof of Claim: Jac⁡(x,u)=Jac⁡(g−1​(A),g−1​(w))=0\Jac(x,u)=\Jac(g^{-1}(A),g^{-1}(w))=0, since Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 (it is clear that if AA and ww are algebraically dependent over DD, then g−1​(A)g^{-1}(A) and g−1​(w)g^{-1}(w) are also algebraically dependent over DD). Apply the first step and get that g−1​(w)=u∈D⁡[x]g^{-1}(w)=u\in D[x]. Hence we can write g−1​(w)=d0+d1​x+d2​x2+⋯+dl​xlg^{-1}(w)=d_{0}+d_{1}x+d_{2}x^{2}+\cdots+d_{l}x^{l}, for some d0,d1,d2,…,dl∈Dd_{0},d_{1},d_{2},\ldots,d_{l}\in D. Then, w=g⁡(d0+d1​x+d2​x2+⋯+dl​xl)=g⁡(d0)+g⁡(d1​x)+g⁡(d2​x2)+⋯+g⁡(dl​xl)=g⁡(d0)+g⁡(d1)​g​(x)+g⁡(d2)​g​(x2)+⋯+g⁡(dl)​g​(xl)=d0+d1​A+d2​A2+⋯+dl​Al∈D⁡[A]w=g(d_{0}+d_{1}x+d_{2}x^{2}+\cdots+d_{l}x^{l})=g(d_{0})+g(d_{1}x)+g(d_{2}x^{2})+\cdots+g(d_{l}x^{l})=g(d_{0})+g(d_{1})g(x)+g(d_{2})g(x^{2})+\cdots+g(d_{l})g(x^{l})=d_{0}+d_{1}A+d_{2}A^{2}+\cdots+d_{l}A^{l}\in D[A]. ∎

It is not surprising that we have not succeeded to find a counterexample to the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture, since when we picked an A∈D⁡[x,y]A\in D[x,y] which has a Jacobian mate B∈D⁡[x,y]B\in D[x,y], those AA and BB always defined an automorphism of D⁡[x,y]D[x,y], and for an automorphism of D⁡[x,y]D[x,y] (= AA is part of an automorphism pair) the conjecture holds by Theorem 3.4.

Given a commutative ring RR, denote:

  • •

    J​C​(2,R)JC(2,R): The two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over RR is true, namely, every RR-algebra endomorphism of R⁡[x,y]R[x,y] having an invertible Jacobian (the Jacobian is in R​[x,y]∗=R∗R[x,y]^{*}=R^{*}) is an automorphism of R⁡[x,y]R[x,y].

  • •

    C​C​(2,R)CC(2,R): The two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over RR is true, namely, if Jac⁡(A,B)∈R​[x,y]∗=R∗\Jac(A,B)\in R[x,y]^{*}=R^{*} and Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0 for A,B,w∈R⁡[x,y]A,B,w\in R[x,y], then w∈R⁡[A]w\in R[A].

We have,

Theorem 3.5 (J​C​(2,D)JC(2,D) implies C​C​(2,D)CC(2,D)).

If the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over DD is true, then the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over DD is true.

We do not know if the converse of Theorem 3.5 is true, namely, if a positive answer to the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over DD implies a positive answer to the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over DD.

Proof.

Assume that A∈D⁡[x,y]A\in D[x,y] has a Jacobian mate BB in D⁡[x,y]D[x,y], and w∈D⁡[x,y]w\in D[x,y] satisfies Jac⁡(A,w)=0\Jac(A,w)=0. We must show that w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A]. By assumption, the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over DD is true, so (x,y)↦(A,B)(x,y)\mapsto(A,B) is an automorphism of D⁡[x,y]D[x,y]. Apply Theorem 3.4 and get that w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A]. ∎

Recall  [9, Lemma 1.1.14] which says that J​C​(2,ℂ)JC(2,\mathbb{C}) implies J​C​(2,D)JC(2,D), therefore:

Theorem 3.6.

If the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over ℂ\mathbb{C} is true, then the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over DD is true.

Proof.

J​C​(2,ℂ)⇒J​C​(2,D)⇒C​C​(2,D)JC(2,\mathbb{C})\Rightarrow JC(2,D)\Rightarrow CC(2,D), where the first implication is due to  [9, Lemma 1.1.14], while the second implication is due to Theorem 3.5. ∎

Of course, Theorem 3.5 implies that if there exists an integral domain DD of characteristic zero such that the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over DD is false, then the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over DD is false, and then, by  [9, Lemma 1.1.14], the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over ℂ\mathbb{C} is false.

We suspect that the two-dimensional Centralizer Conjecture over any integral domain of characteristic zero is true, because we ’believe’ that the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture is true.

Finally, we wish to quote A. van den Essen  [10, page 2]: “… All these experiences fed my believe that the Jacobian Conjecture, if true at all, would be difficult to generalize, since it felt like a kind of optimal statement”.

4  Non-commutative analog: The first Weyl algebra

By definition, the nn’th Weyl algebra An​(k)A_{n}(k) is the unital associative kk-algebra generated by 2​n2n elements X1,…,Xn,Y1,…,YnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n},Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{n} subject to the following defining relations: [Yi,Xj]=δi​j[Y_{i},X_{j}]=\delta_{ij}, [Xi,Xj]=0[X_{i},X_{j}]=0 and [Yi,Yj]=0[Y_{i},Y_{j}]=0, where δi​j\delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta. When n=1n=1, we will denote the generators by X,YX,Y instead of by X1,Y1X_{1},Y_{1}.

The first Weyl algebra, A1​(k)A_{1}(k), was first studied by Dirac  [7]. In  [8], Dixmier posed six questions concerning A1​(k)A_{1}(k), kk is a field of characteristic zero. The first question asked if every kk-algebra endomorphism of A1​(k)A_{1}(k) is an automorphism of A1​(k)A_{1}(k); this is known as Dixmier Conjecture.

Given a commutative ring RR, denote:

  • •

    J​C​(n,R)JC(n,R): The nn-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over RR is true, namely, every RR-algebra endomorphism of R⁡[x1,…,xn]R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] having an invertible Jacobian (the Jacobian is in R​[x1,…,xn]∗=R∗R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]^{*}=R^{*}) is an automorphism of R⁡[x1,…,xn]R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}].

  • •

    D​C​(n,R)DC(n,R): The nn’th Dixmier Conjecture over RR is true, namely, every RR-algebra endomorphism of An​(R)A_{n}(R) is an automorphism of An​(R)A_{n}(R).

  • •

    J​C​(∞,R)JC(\infty,R): For all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, the nn-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over RR is true.

  • •

    D​C​(∞,R)DC(\infty,R): For all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, the nn’th Dixmier Conjecture over RR is true.

There is a well-known connection between the Jacobian Conjecture and the Dixmier Conjecture, which says the following: For all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}:

  • (i)

    D​C​(n,k)DC(n,k) ⇒\Rightarrow J​C​(n,k)JC(n,k).

  • (ii)

    J​C​(2​n,k)JC(2n,k) ⇒\Rightarrow D​C​(n,k)DC(n,k).

The first result can be found in  [9, Theorem 4.2.8] and in  [3, page 297] (immediately after Proposition 2.3). The second result was proved independently by Y. Tsuchimoto  [21] and by A. Belov-Kanel and M. Kontsevich  [5]. There exist additional proofs due to V. V. Bavula  [4], and due to K. Adjamagbo and A. van den Essen  [1]. From (i)(i) and (i​i)(ii) it is clear that J​C​(∞,k)JC(\infty,k) is equivalent to D​C​(∞,k)DC(\infty,k).

In the non-commutative algebra A1​(k)A_{1}(k), denote the centralizer of an element PP by Cent⁡(P)\Cent(P) (= all the elements in A1​(k)A_{1}(k) which commute with PP).

An analog result in A1​(k)A_{1}(k) to CMW’s result in k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] exists, and is due to J. A. Guccione, J. J. Guccione and C. Valqui, namely:

Theorem 4.1 (Analog of CMW’s theorem over kk).

If P,Q∈A1​(k)P,Q\in A_{1}(k) satisfy [Q,P]∈A1​(k)∗=k∗[Q,P]\in A_{1}(k)^{*}=k^{*}, then Cent⁡(P)=k⁡[P]\Cent(P)=k[P].

Proof.

See  [11, Theorem 2.11]. ∎

Notice that the non-commutative case  [11, Theorem 2.11] is already over kk, while the commutative case  [6, Theorem 1] is over ℂ\mathbb{C} and we showed in Theorem 2.3 and in Proposition 2.6 that ℂ\mathbb{C} can be replaced by kk.

Remark 4.2.

It seems that none of the proofs of Theorem 2.3 and Proposition 2.6 has a non-commutative version:

  • •

    The proof of Theorem 2.3 is based on Formanek’s observation, Proposition 2.1, and on Jacobi’s theorem, Theorem 2.2 (2)(2), which together say the following: Assume that C,D∈k⁡[x,y]C,D\in k[x,y] satisfy Jac⁡(C,D)=0\Jac(C,D)=0. Then there exist h∈k⁡[x,y]h\in k[x,y] and u⁡(t),v⁡(t)∈k⁡[t]u(t),v(t)\in k[t], such that C=u⁡(h)C=u(h) and D=v⁡(h)D=v(h). However, there exists a known counterexample due to Dixmier  [8] to this result in the non-commutative case, namely, there exist C,D∈A1​(k)C,D\in A_{1}(k) satisfying [C,D]=0[C,D]=0, but there exist no h∈A1​(k)h\in A_{1}(k) and u⁡(t),v⁡(t)∈k⁡[t]u(t),v(t)\in k[t], such that C=u⁡(h)C=u(h) and D=v⁡(h)D=v(h). For more details on the counterexample, see  [15] and  [18].

  • •

    The proof of Proposition 2.6 is based on the original CMW’s theorem; the proof of the original CMW’s theorem uses results concerning ℂ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y] (such as extension of derivations), and we do not know if those results have non-commutative analogs.

CMW’s theorem over kk implies Theorem 3.1, and similarly, the analog of CMW’s theorem over kk, Theorem 4.1, implies the following analog of Theorem 3.1:

Theorem 4.3.

Suppose [A,B]∈A1​(D)∗=D∗[A,B]\in A_{1}(D)^{*}=D^{*} and [A,w]=0[A,w]=0 for A,B,w∈A1​(D)A,B,w\in A_{1}(D). Then w∈Q​(D)​[A]w\in Q(D)[A].

Proof.

A,B∈A1​(D)⊂A1​(Q⁡(D))A,B\in A_{1}(D)\subset A_{1}(Q(D)) satisfy [A,B]∈D∗⊂Q​(D)∗[A,B]\in D^{*}\subset Q(D)^{*} and w∈A1​(D)⊂A1​(Q⁡(D))w\in A_{1}(D)\subset A_{1}(Q(D)) satisfies [A,w]=0[A,w]=0. We can apply Theorem 4.1 (Q⁡(D)Q(D) is a field of characteristic zero) and obtain that w∈Q​(D)​[A]w\in Q(D)[A]. ∎

We conjecture the non-commutative analog of Conjecture 3.2:

Conjecture 4.4 (The (first) Centralizer Conjecture over DD).

Suppose [A,B]∈A1​(D)∗=D∗[A,B]\in A_{1}(D)^{*}=D^{*} and [A,w]=0[A,w]=0 for A,B,w∈A1​(D)A,B,w\in A_{1}(D). Then w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A].

The following useful equation will be applied in Examples 4.6 and in the proof of Theorem 4.7.

Lemma 4.5 (Useful equation).

For all t⁡(Y)∈k⁡[Y]t(Y)\in k[Y] and i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}: [t⁡(Y),Xi]=i​Xi−1​t′​(Y)+(i2)​Xi−2​t′′​(Y)+…[t(Y),X^{i}]=iX^{i-1}t^{\prime}(Y)+\binom{i}{2}X^{i-2}t^{\prime\prime}(Y)+\dots.

In particular, this equation is valid for t⁡(Y)∈D⁡[Y]t(Y)\in D[Y] (since t⁡(Y)∈D⁡[Y]⊂Q⁡(D)​[Y]t(Y)\in D[Y]\subset Q(D)[Y]).

Proof.

See  [12, Proposition 1.6]. ∎

The analog of Examples 3.3 is:

The (first) Centralizer Conjecture has a positive answer (at least) in the following two special cases:

  • •

    First special case: DD is, in addition, a field; this is the analog of CMW’s theorem over kk, Theorem 4.1.

Second step AA arbitrary: The general case can be obtained from the special case A=XA=X.

Claim: u:=g−1​(w)u:=g^{-1}(w) is in the centralizer of XX.

Proof of Claim: [X,u]=[g−1​(A),g−1​(w)][X,u]=[g^{-1}(A),g^{-1}(w)] =g−1​(A)​g−1​(w)−g−1​(w)​g−1​(A)=g^{-1}(A)g^{-1}(w)-g^{-1}(w)g^{-1}(A) =g−1​(A​w)−g−1​(w​A)=g−1​(A​w−w​A)=g^{-1}(Aw)-g^{-1}(wA)=g^{-1}(Aw-wA) =g−1​([A,w])=g−1​(0)=0=g^{-1}([A,w])=g^{-1}(0)=0. Apply the first step and get that g−1​(w)=u∈D⁡[X]g^{-1}(w)=u\in D[X]. Hence we can write g−1​(w)=d0+d1​X+d2​X2+⋯+dl​Xlg^{-1}(w)=d_{0}+d_{1}X+d_{2}X^{2}+\cdots+d_{l}X^{l}, for some d0,d1,d2,…,dl∈Dd_{0},d_{1},d_{2},\ldots,d_{l}\in D. Then, w=g⁡(d0+d1​X+d2​X2+⋯+dl​Xl)=g⁡(d0)+g⁡(d1​X)+g⁡(d2​X2)+⋯+g⁡(dl​Xl)=g⁡(d0)+g⁡(d1)​g​(X)+g⁡(d2)​g​(X2)+⋯+g⁡(dl)​g​(Xl)=d0+d1​A+d2​A2+⋯+dl​Al∈D⁡[A]w=g(d_{0}+d_{1}X+d_{2}X^{2}+\cdots+d_{l}X^{l})=g(d_{0})+g(d_{1}X)+g(d_{2}X^{2})+\cdots+g(d_{l}X^{l})=g(d_{0})+g(d_{1})g(X)+g(d_{2})g(X^{2})+\cdots+g(d_{l})g(X^{l})=d_{0}+d_{1}A+d_{2}A^{2}+\cdots+d_{l}A^{l}\in D[A]. ∎

We have an analog to Theorem 3.5:

Theorem 4.8.

If the first Dixmier Conjecture over DD is true, then the (first) Centralizer Conjecture over DD is true.

We do not know if the converse of Theorem 4.8 is true, namely, if a positive answer to the (first) Centralizer Conjecture over DD implies a positive answer to the first Dixmier Conjecture over DD.

Proof.

Assume that A∈A1​(D)A\in A_{1}(D) has a Dixmier mate BB in A1​(D)A_{1}(D), and w∈A1​(D)w\in A_{1}(D) satisfies [A,w]=0[A,w]=0. We must show that w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A]. By assumption, the first Dixmier Conjecture over DD is true, so (X,Y)↦(A,λ​B)(X,Y)\mapsto(A,\lambda B), λ=[A,B]−1\lambda=[A,B]^{-1}, is an automorphism of A1​(D)A_{1}(D). Apply Theorem 4.7 and get that w∈D⁡[A]w\in D[A]. ∎

We do not know if an analog of  [9, Lemma 1.1.14] exists, hence we do not know how to obtain an analog of Theorem 3.6.

Of course, Theorem 4.8 implies that if there exists an integral domain DD of characteristic zero such that the first Centralizer Conjecture over DD is false, then the first Dixmier Conjecture over DD is false, namely, there exists A,B∈A1​(D)A,B\in A_{1}(D), [B,A]=1[B,A]=1 and (X,Y)↦(A,B)(X,Y)\mapsto(A,B) is not an automorphism of A1​(D)A_{1}(D). We have recalled above in (i​i)(ii) that J​C​(2​n,k)JC(2n,k) ⇒\Rightarrow D​C​(n,k)DC(n,k). If this implication is also valid if we replace kk by DD, namely, J​C​(2​n,D)JC(2n,D) ⇒\Rightarrow D​C​(n,D)DC(n,D), then, in particular, J​C​(2,D)JC(2,D) ⇒\Rightarrow D​C​(1,D)DC(1,D). Therefore, if the first Dixmier Conjecture over DD is false, then the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over DD is false, and then by  [9, Lemma 1.1.14], the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture over ℂ\mathbb{C} is false.
